title: Dark matter searches are becoming a test of competing possibilities
excerpt: Liquid xenon, silicon sensors, microwave cavities and seasonal comparisons are probing different dark matter hypotheses. Discover more
content:
Liquid xenon, silicon sensors, microwave cavities and seasonal comparisons are probing different dark matter hypotheses. Understanding their reach is essential to interpreting both null results and intriguing events.

A dark matter detector can become more informative without discovering dark matter. It can rule out an interaction that should have appeared, reveal a background that previously escaped notice, or show that an apparent signal does not recur in another material or location. The scientific challenge is to distinguish these outcomes without reducing a diverse field to an annual announcement that the particle remains missing.

That distinction is particularly timely. In September 2026, the LUX-ZEPLIN collaboration reported an unusual event in a search extending to higher nuclear recoil energies. Elsewhere, sodium iodide experiments are testing a longstanding annual modulation claim, while semiconductor and microwave detectors examine candidates that behave very differently from conventional weakly interacting massive particles. These are connected investigations, but they are not interchangeable attempts to detect one agreed object.

What a xenon result excludes

LUX-ZEPLIN, usually called LZ, searches for tiny recoils of xenon nuclei following a possible collision with a dark matter particle. Its analysis published in 2025 used 4.2 tonne-years of exposure, corresponding to 280 live days. The data constrained nuclear scattering by hypothetical weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs, within the interaction models analysed. Exposure combines the amount of usable target material with observing time; it does not describe a particle’s mass.

A reported exclusion is therefore conditional. It applies to a candidate mass, an interaction strength and assumptions about the surrounding dark matter population. A particle interacting primarily with electrons, or through a different nuclear response, may produce another signature. Even within a particular WIMP model, lowering the interaction strength can move a candidate beyond the experiment’s present reach.

This is why a null search cannot establish that dark matter does not exist. It does remove possibilities that were testable. The useful comparison between experiments is the territory of mass and interaction strength they investigate, together with the assumptions needed to connect their results.

One unusual event deserves a precise description

LZ’s September 2026 preprint examined an extended recoil window reaching approximately 270 kiloelectronvolts. Using 2.84 tonne-years of exposure, the team identified one event consistent with a nuclear recoil of 248 kiloelectronvolts, with separate statistical and systematic uncertainties of 23 kiloelectronvolts each. The analysis considered interactions for which higher-energy recoils can be more prominent than in the conventional spin-independent search.

The maximum local significance was 3.4 standard deviations, but the global significance was 2.6 after accounting for the multiple possibilities examined. This look-elsewhere adjustment recognises that a search with more opportunities to find an unusual feature has a greater chance of encountering one. The preprint discusses rare background configurations and does not establish a dark matter discovery.

The productive response is a targeted investigation of that event’s possible origins. Neither dismissing it because previous searches were null nor treating it as the missing particle follows from the evidence. Its importance depends on what further data and background studies show.

Neutrinos enter the same detectors

Increasing sensitivity also exposes a background that cannot be removed by putting more rock above the experiment. Neutrinos can scatter from nuclei and produce signals resembling some dark matter interactions. XENONnT reported an indication of this process from solar boron-8 neutrinos in 2024. Its analysis observed 37 events above a 0.5-kiloelectronvolt threshold, against an expected background of about 26.4 events, yielding a significance of 2.73 standard deviations.

The result is evidence of growing sensitivity to a known physical process, rather than evidence for dark matter. It also makes the practical meaning of the often discussed neutrino fog clearer. Some candidate signals become harder to distinguish statistically from neutrino recoils. The challenge depends on particle mass, interaction and detector performance; it is not a single absolute barrier beyond which every search stops.

Different target materials and complementary observables become especially valuable in this regime. A background that resembles one candidate in one detector need not reproduce the full pattern expected across several experiments.

Small sensors reach a different population

For sufficiently light candidates, the energy deposited in a heavy nucleus may be too small to register. Semiconductor searches can instead look for very small ionisation signals. SENSEI’s first SNOLAB result used six specially designed Skipper charge-coupled devices, which allow repeated measurements of the charge in a pixel. After masking unsuitable data, the analysis retained an exposure of 100.72 gram-days.

The team observed 55 two-electron events, four three-electron events and none containing four to ten electrons. It examined possible instrumental origins and used the data to constrain dark matter interactions, rather than labelling the low-charge events as a discovery. This example illustrates why target mass alone is a poor measure of scientific reach. A small sensor capable of resolving a few electrons can explore interactions inaccessible to a much larger detector with a higher threshold.

The engineering priorities consequently change. Sensor defects, unwanted charge and the reliability of event selection can matter more than simply adding material. Comparing tonnes with grams without considering the signal being sought misses the reason both approaches exist.

Testing an annual pattern in another laboratory

The ANAIS-112 experiment in Spain asks a different question: can another sodium iodide detector reproduce the annual modulation reported by DAMA/LIBRA in Italy? Its six-year analysis found results incompatible with the DAMA/LIBRA modulation at approximately four standard deviations. Using the same target material reduces the particle-model dependence involved in comparing sodium iodide with xenon. The researchers nevertheless highlighted detector response to nuclear recoils as an uncertainty requiring attention. ANAIS six-year analysis

SABRE South adds geographical leverage. Its design combines very pure sodium iodide crystals with systems that identify accompanying radiation and cosmic-ray activity. Comparing observations from opposite hemispheres can help separate a galactic modulation from effects associated with local seasons. That logic requires stable detector operation and measured backgrounds; latitude alone cannot identify a particle.

A September 2026 presentation described SABRE South as being in construction and commissioning, with underground measurements including the cosmic-ray muon flux. That is a useful operational milestone, but it is not a completed test of the dark matter modulation.

Listening for axions

Axion searches require another kind of apparatus. ADMX uses a magnetic field and a microwave resonator to look for axion conversion into photons. Cooling and very low-noise amplification help reveal the exceptionally weak signal. Its 2025 paper reported a search between 1.10 and 1.31 gigahertz, constraining a benchmark class of axion models without finding an axion signal.

The frequency range corresponds to a particular mass interval, and sensitivity depends on the assumed axion-photon coupling and local axion abundance. A successful exclusion in that interval cannot eliminate every axion model. Scanning another frequency or reaching a weaker coupling is a distinct scientific advance, even when the hardware resembles the previous experiment.

Taken together, these programmes show why dark matter research needs both breadth and repetition. Repetition tests whether a claimed pattern survives another detector. Breadth tests whether the original choice of particle and interaction was too narrow. The most convincing future signal would also generate specific predictions that another experiment could attempt to verify.

For Europe’s laboratories and suppliers, the resulting portfolio spans radiopure materials, cryogenics, semiconductor fabrication, low-noise electronics and long-term underground operation. Its coherence comes from the physics questions connecting those technologies. An exclusion, a calibration result and an unexplained event each advance the programme differently; keeping those differences visible allows the next investment or measurement to address the actual remaining uncertainty.

A useful next step after a possible signal is to calculate its expected consequences elsewhere before inspecting new data. Would another target see a related recoil spectrum? Would the event rate change in a predictable way as the Earth moves? Would a detector with a different threshold retain sensitivity? Those questions turn an isolated anomaly into a programme of discriminating measurements. They also expose situations in which two apparently conflicting experiments are testing different assumptions. Shared analysis information therefore has scientific value alongside new equipment: it allows independent teams to test the same explanation without rebuilding the same apparatus.
